node.label: Silvia Federici
node.date_label: Wages against Housework (1975) · Caliban and the Witch (2004) · Revolution at Point Zero (2012) · “Social reproduction theory” (2019)
node.description: In Caliban and the Witch (2004), Silvia Federici argues that capitalism developed through the coercive reorganization of reproduction, with the witch-hunts and the subordination of women central to primitive accumulation. She treats reproductive labour as a source of capitalist wealth whose unpaid status helps conceal its exploitation, a framework also developed in Revolution at Point Zero (2012). In Socialism & Democracy no. 41 (July 2006), Hester Eisenstein praises the book’s feminist reinterpretation of capitalism but criticizes its idealization of communal rural life and its one-sided assessment of capitalist development. Federici’s account connects women’s history to class relations while disputing Marx’s treatment of primitive accumulation and Foucault’s account of bodily discipline. Her 2019 intervention in social reproduction theory defends the productivity of unpaid work against competing Marxist interpretations.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Wages against Housework (1975); Il Grande Calibano (1984), with Leopoldina Fortunati; Caliban and the Witch: Women, the Body and Primitive Accumulation (2004; Spanish translation 2010; revised English edition 2014); Revolution at Point Zero: Housework, Reproduction, and Feminist Struggle (2012; expanded second edition 2020); “Social reproduction theory: History, issues and present challenges” (2019).
node.scope_note: Complete preface and introduction plus selected chapter passages read in the authorized 2010 Spanish translation of Caliban and the Witch; original English text and remaining chapters unread. Complete Eisenstein review and 2019 Radical Philosophy essay read. Revolution at Point Zero and the other books identified through publisher, university or bibliographic records, not read in full. Selected Commons essay passages read; final pages and notes not completely read. The 2026 interview’s opening is accessible; remainder paywalled.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Caliban and the Witch (2004), Federici criticizes Marx’s account of primitive accumulation for omitting women’s reproductive labour and the witch-hunts, and disputes its emancipatory assessment of capitalist development.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary introduction, Spanish 2010 translation, printed pp. 22–24 (PDF pp. 19–21): “ausentes en Marx”. Read as Federici’s criticism of Capital I (1867), not an adjudication of Marx’s whole corpus. English original and Capital not freshly read.
proposed_edges.map_label: Reproduction and violence in primitive accumulation

proposed_edges.relationship: In Caliban and the Witch (2004), Federici argues that Foucault’s histories of bodily discipline and sexuality neglect reproductive labour, sexual differentiation and witch-hunting, obscuring the connection between biopower and capital accumulation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary preface p. 17 and introduction pp. 29–31, Spanish 2010 translation (PDF pp. 14, 26–28): “omisión de la caza de brujas”. Her retrospective preface also attributes the earlier criticism to the coauthored Il Grande Calibano (1984); the proposed claim is the 2004 restatement. No Foucault reply asserted; his original texts not freshly read.
proposed_edges.map_label: Questions the asexual subject of bodily discipline

proposed_edges.relationship: In Caliban and the Witch (2004), Federici credits Joan Kelly’s “Did Women Have a Renaissance?” (1977; cited in its 1984 collected form) with challenging conventional periodization and identifies it among the works on which her own study builds.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary introduction, Spanish translation pp. 24–25 (PDF pp. 21–22), explicitly names Kelly and says the book “se basa en estos trabajos”. Existing source kelly_renaissance supplies the original 1977 date; Federici cites the 1984 collection. Kelly’s essay not freshly read. This is an acknowledged intellectual resource, not supervision or personal collaboration.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Caliban and the Witch (2004), Federici values Merchant’s The Death of Nature (1980) but disputes making scientific rationalism or mechanism the immediate cause of the witch-hunts, emphasizing the imposition of capitalist social discipline.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary Spanish translation, pp. 279–281 (PDF pp. 276–278), read with the appreciative introduction p. 25: “Ni el racionalismo ni el mecanicismo”. Federici argues that organic cosmologies also accommodated domination. Critique is qualified by explicit praise; Merchant’s complete book and any reply unread. Existing Merchant source used for original 1980 metadata only.
proposed_edges.map_label: Qualifies Merchant’s explanation of the witch-hunts

proposed_edges.relationship: In Caliban and the Witch (2004), Federici cites Clark’s Working Life of Women in the Seventeenth Century (1919; 1968 reprint) but argues that midwives’ exclusion must be explained through control of reproduction as well as women’s loss of professional training.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary Spanish translation p. 252 (PDF p. 249), Clark quotation followed immediately by Federici’s objection to “desprofesionalización femenina”. Bibliography identifies Clark’s 1968 [1919] edition; existing clark_working_primary confirms the original title/date. This narrowly concerns the quoted explanation, not a rejection of Clark’s complete work. Clark’s occupational chapter not freshly read.
proposed_edges.map_label: Beyond deprofessionalization in the history of midwifery

proposed_edges.relationship: Caliban and the Witch (2004) reinterprets women’s history through changes in reproductive labour, bodily coercion and resistance during the transition to capitalism.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary Spanish introduction pp. 21–26 and 29–30 read. Explicitly situates the intervention within women’s history while opposing a history separated from male workers. This is Federici’s historical framework; no field founding or consensus claim. Whole book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Caliban and the Witch (2004), Federici interprets femininity and masculinity through the historical construction of a sexual division of labour and connects gender hierarchy to class relations.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary preface p. 17 and introduction pp. 26–27, Spanish translation, read in full. The passage explicitly addresses the gender/class division and the analytical category women. Contribution records a disputed materialist interpretation, not a definition binding on gender history. English original unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Historically constructed gender and class relations

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Social reproduction theory” (2019), Federici argues that unpaid housework and other unwaged or unfree labour belong within the analysis of capitalist exploitation, and treats wages as instruments that organize labour hierarchies.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete primary journal HTML, printed pp. 55–57; paragraphs beginning What made, It was discovering and It was unmasking: “other unpaid and un-free labourers”. The labour-history connection is editorial placement of an explicit argument about labour and exploitation, not a claim that the essay is an empirical labour history or that the field accepts her value theory.
proposed_edges.map_label: Unpaid work and the hierarchy of wages

proposed_edges.relationship: Caliban and the Witch (2004) intervenes in the transition-to-capitalism debate by treating the reorganization of reproduction and the witch-hunts as constitutive of primitive accumulation and by arguing that dispossessive violence recurs within capitalism.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary Spanish introduction pp. 21–24 and 31 read. The introduction explicitly places the book in the transition debate and sets out its differences from Marx; the formulation is Federici’s contested argument. This debate edge concerns her explanatory intervention, distinct from the person-directed Marx critique. Original English book and other participants’ texts unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: A feminist account of the transition to capitalism
